justifications.c1: Independent EA and trade-press figures per case of £4,300 (Rutterford, search-confirmed), £5,531 (s.201 false return) and over £7,000 (Cambridgeshire), above £2k and above 5x a plausible TCO; but these are rare prosecutions, often for deliberate or unlicensed abstraction a logger would not prevent, and no crop-loss cost of a missed HoF stop or cap was found.
justifications.c2: Each licence sets the recording frequency and most require an annual return, with nil returns (gov.uk, search-confirmed); weekly and monthly return types exist (EA spreadsheet guide), but the typical reading frequency for irrigation licences and the number of HoF stops per season were not sourced.
justifications.c3: A documented manual routine (meter readings, online or spreadsheet returns, meter flow checks, an irrigation specialist role recording use for compliance), but no hours or £ cost of reading and returns preparation was found.
justifications.c4: Licence conditions under the Water Resources Act 1991 require meters, records and returns (gov.uk, search-confirmed), with enforcement in this niche: Rutterford was prosecuted for over-abstraction, not keeping records and not calibrating meters (EA release, search-confirmed), plus a s.201 false-return case and 70 enforcement actions; telemetry itself is not required.
justifications.c5: The licence holder is the party prosecuted; Irrigation Manager (Barfoots, mapping inferred) and Irrigation Specialist adverts cover abstraction compliance, but none states a purchasing budget.
justifications.c6: Meter suppliers (Bell Flow 'automated abstraction compliance', DMS) and land agents (Savills) serve this market, but Bell Flow is closer to a competitor than a site-visiting channel, and no irrigation dealer or the UK Irrigation Association bundles telemetry (recorded not found).
justifications.c7: Adjacent telemetry exists (Bell Flow, McCrometer, ABB, CropX in AU, mandatory metering in NZ), but there are no UK prices or customer counts, and the gap (no UK product turning pulses into licence tracking and EA returns) is evidenced only by absence.
justifications.c8: Reading an existing meter's pulse output avoids metrology approval; an off-the-shelf pulse logger costs £105–112 ex VAT (RS, search-confirmed; Bluetooth, not LPWAN) and a LoRaWAN pulse node exists unpriced; older meters may lack pulse outputs and remote boreholes may lack coverage.
justifications.c9: Records and annual returns recur on a statutory licence schedule (search-confirmed) and HoF alerts recur each dry season, but no comparable subscription price was found, which caps the score below 7.
justifications.c10: Regulator enforcement (EA press releases on Norfolk and Cambridgeshire), extensive trade press (Farmers Weekly, FarmingUK, Farmers Guardian, Farmers Guide) and a whistleblower news piece; no first-hand farmer complaints were found.

weakest: The money at stake per farm is modest and rare (fines of £4k–£7k, mostly for deliberate abstraction) and no comparable UK subscription price or product proves willingness to pay.
